title: [C1T1] - A spark, a flint: How to light a fire

parts.passageHtml:
{[The control of fire was the first and perhaps greatest of humanity’s steps towards a life-enhancing technology.][290602]}

{[To early man, the fire was a gift randomly delivered from lightning, forest fire or burning lava.][290620]} {[The earliest peoples, who are unable to make flame for themselves, probably stored fire by keeping slow burning logs alight or by carrying charcoal in pots.][290636]}

{[How and where man learnt how to produce flame at will is unknown.][290665]} {[Studies of primitive societies suggest that the earliest method of making fire was through friction.][290679]} {[European peasants would insert a wooden drill in a round hole and rotate it briskly between their palms.][290695]}

{[Fire-lighting was revolutionized by the discovery of phosphorus, isolated in 1669 by a German alchemist.][290713]} {[Impressed by the combustibility of phosphorus, several 17th-century chemists used it to manufacture fire-lighting devices.][290728]} {[With phosphorus costing the equivalent of several hundred pounds per ounce, the first matches were expensive.][290744]}

{[The first matches resembling those used today were made in 1827 by John Walker, an English pharmacist who borrowed the formula from a military rocket-maker called Congreve.][290762]} {[Congreve matches were splints coated with sulfur and tipped with potassium chlorate.][290789]} {[To light them, the user drew them quickly through folded glass paper.][290802]}

{[Later, a Swedish chemist, Pasch, had discovered non-toxic red or amorphous phosphorus, a development exploited commercially by his compatriot J E Lundstrom in 1885.][290816]} {[Lundstrom’s safety matches were safe because the red phosphorus was non-toxic; it was painted on to the striking surface instead of the match tip, which contained potassium chlorate with a relatively high ignition temperature of 182 degrees centigrade.][290841]}

{[America lagged behind Europe in matching technology and safety standards.][290880]}

{[However, the Americans did contribute to match technology and marketing.][290892]} {[In 1892 the Diamond Match Company pioneered book matches.][290903]} {[This innovation started to gain in popularity after 1896, when a brewery had the novel idea of advertising its product in matchbooks.][290913]} {[Today book matches are the most widely used type in the US, with 90 percent handed out free by hotels, restaurants and others.][290934]}

{[Other American innovations include an anti-after-glow solution to prevent the match from smoldering after it has been blown out; and the waterproof match, which lights after eight hours in water.][290958]}

Questions 9 - 13:

Write your answers in boxes 9-13 on your answer sheet.

questions.explanationHtml:
9

Đoạn 8 (That was 62 years after a Swedish chemist called Pasch had discovered non-toxic red or amorphous phosphorus, a development exploited commercially by Pasch’s compatriot J E Lundstrom in 1885. Lundstrom’s safety matches were safe because the red phosphorus was non-toxic;...)

C (“Ludstrom’s safety match” sử dụng “red phosphorus” - phốt phô đỏ và chất này “non-toxic” không độc hại → “less poisonous type of phosphorus” ít độc hại hơn các loại diêm trước đó)

questions.text: identical to a previous type of match
questions.explanationHtml:
10

Đoạn 7 (Walker never patented his invention, and three years later it was copied by Samuel Jones, who marketed his product as Lucifers)

D (“Walker là người đầu tiên tạo ra diêm nhưng ông không đăng kí bản quyền → sản phẩm bị “copied” sao chép bởi “Samuel Jones” và ông này đặt tên là diêm “Lucifers”

11

Đoạn 7 (About the same time, a French chemistry student called Charles Sauria produced the first “strike-anywhere” match by substituting white phosphorus for the potassium chlorate in the Walker formula. However, since white phosphorus is a deadly poison, from 1845 match-makers exposed to its fumes succumbed to necrosis, a disease that eats away jaw-bones.)

E (diêm “strike-anywhere” rất tiện lợi tuy nhiên chứa chất “white phosphorus” - phốt phô trắng → đây là chất “deadly poisonous” độc hại chết người → gây ra bệnh “necrosis” sẽ ăn mòn xương hàm “jaw-bones”)

questions.text: first to look like modern matches
questions.explanationHtml:
12

Đoạn 5 (The first matches resembling those used today were made in 1827 by John Walker, an English pharmacist who borrowed the formula from a military rocket-maker called Congreve)

C (paraphrase “resembling” thành “look like” trong đề → que diêm đầu tiên giống với ngày nay nhất được tạo ra bởi Walker, ông này mượn công thức của một ông chế tên lửa tên là Congreve→ đặt tên diêm “Congreves”)

13

Đoạn 8 (The Americans, however, can claim several “firsts'' in match technology and marketing. In 1892 the Diamond Match Company pioneered book matches. The innovation didn’t catch on until after 1896, when a brewery had the novel idea of advertising its product in matchbooks.)

G
